1:1.t: The order of the twelve prophets among the Seventy translators is not the same as that which is kept in the Hebrew truth. For they put Amos second, Micah third, Joel fourth, Obadiah fifth, Jonah sixth, Nahum seventh, Habakkuk eighth, Zephaniah ninth, Haggai tenth, Zechariah eleventh, Malachi twelfth; but the Hebrews, after Hosea, who is first among both, read Joel second, Amos third, Obadiah fourth, Jonah fifth, Micah sixth, Nahum seventh, Habakkuk eighth, Zephaniah ninth, Haggai tenth, Zechariah eleventh, and twelfth, who is also the last, Malachi. And since we have once enumerated all the prophets of the one volume, it seems useful to us to note briefly the ἐτυμολογίας (etymologies) of each, both in Greek and in Latin. Hosea means σώζων, whom we can call one who saves. Joel ἀρχόμενος, that is, beginning. Amos βαστάζων, which among the Latins is called carrying. Obadiah δοῦλος Κυρίου, that is, servant of the Lord. Jonah περιστερὰ, that is, dove. […]

The word of the Lord which was made to Joel, the son of Phatuel. The Seventy translators rendered Bathuel for Phatuel, which in Hebrew has no meaning at all. But Phatuel is rendered into our language as breadth of God, or God opening, as we read in Mark that the Savior said to the deaf and dumb man: Ephpheta, which is, be opened. For since he could say with the Apostle: Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians, our heart is enlarged, and heard from the Lord: Make wide your mouth, and I will fill it; and since this very opening of the mouth is not in the power of man but in the power of God, as Paul says: A great and evident door has been opened to me; but there are many adversaries; therefore he is called God opening. And since the saint always makes progress, knowing in part and prophesying in part, until that which is perfect comes, he who is begotten of breadth and opening is called Joel, which in our language means beginning, or is God, as the Apostle says: Brothers, I do not consider that I have laid hold of it; […]

1:2.t: Hear this, old men, and perceive with your ears, all inhabitants of the earth, if this has happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers; tell of this to your sons, and your sons to their sons, and their sons to another generation. LXX: Hear these things, old men, and perceive with your ears, all inhabitants of the earth, if such things have happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers; for these things, tell your sons, and your sons their sons, and their sons to another generation. The old men are commanded to hear, the inhabitants of the earth to perceive with their ears. To the old men it is not said: Hear, all; to the inhabitants of the earth is added: Perceive with your ears, all. But hearing in the holy Scriptures is not that which sounds in the ear, but that which is perceived by the heart, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. […]

1:3.t: Therefore, both old men and inhabitants of the earth, tell it to your sons and to your posterity: let him who is an old man teach his children the mysteries; let him who is an inhabitant of the earth tell the simple history. Hence to this very day we who believe in Christ, from whose eyes the veil has been taken away with Moses, and of whom it is said: The gray hairs of a man are his wisdom, tell our sons things secret and wonderful. But the Jews, who dwell on the earth, speak earthly things that cling to the ground, of whom it is written: He who is of the earth speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all.

1:4.t: What the caterpillar left, the locust has eaten, and what the locust left, the cankerworm has eaten, and what the cankerworm left, the blight has eaten. LXX: likewise. The narration follows the exordium: there, to make the hearer attentive, he promised that he would say great and incredible things, which neither ancient history knew nor the present age knew to have happened. Here he has set down the caterpillar, and the locust, and the cankerworm, and the blight, so that things each of which rarely happens may be recorded as having happened all at once, and may therefore be wonderful. The caterpillar, which in Hebrew is called gezem, in Greek κάμπη, the Hebrews interpret as the Assyrians, the Babylonians and the Chaldeans, who, coming forth from one region of the world, laid waste everything belonging to the ten tribes as well as to the two, that is, to the Israelite people. The locust they interpret as the Medes and Persians, who, after the overthrow of the empire of the Chaldeans, held the Jews captive. […]

We certainly know that in clouds of smoke, when some are fading away above, others rise up from below. So too in carnal thoughts, though some evil desires pass away, yet others succeed. But frequently the wretched mind beholds what has already passed but does not behold where it is still detained. It rejoices in being no longer subject to some sins but neglects to be careful and to lament because others have succeeded in their place, to which perhaps it yields more sinfully. And so it is that while some sins pass away and others succeed, the heart of the reprobate is possessed without intermission by this serpent. Therefore it is well said by the prophet Joel: "That which the palmer-worm has left, the locust has eaten; and that which the locust has left, the canker-worm has eaten; and that which the canker-worm has left, the mildew has eaten."
1:4.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book XXXIII

1:5.t: Wake up, you drunkards; and weep and howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth. LXX: Awake, you who are drunk with your wine; and wail and lament, all you who drink wine in drunkenness, because it has been taken away from your mouth. As old men and elders we ought to hear: nothing so makes one drunk as the perturbation of the mind. There is a sorrow that leads to death: this is a drunkenness to be abhorred. There is an anger that does not work the righteousness of God, and, being very near to madness, it makes a man not master of his own mind, so much that the lips tremble, the teeth chatter, the face changes with pallor. And rightly is that saying of Archytas of Tarentum praised, who, when he was angry with his steward, said: I would kill you now, he said, if I were not angry. What shall I say of joy and pleasure, and above all of love, which blinds the eyes of the heart and permits the lover to think of nothing but what he loves? […]

1:6.t: How then are we to be freed from this pest? If we can drink a potion that is able to kill the worms within us and the serpents. And of what nature, it will be asked, may this potion be, that hath such power? The precious Blood of Christ, if it be received with full assurance, for this will have power to extinguish every disease; and together with this the divine Scriptures carefully heard, and almsgiving added to our hearing; for by means of all these things we shall be enabled to mortify the affections that mar our soul. And then only shall we live; for now surely we are in no better state than the dead: forasmuch as it cannot be, that while those passions live, we should live too, but we must necessarily perish. And unless we first kill them here, they will be sure to kill us in the other life; or rather before that death they will exact of us, even here, the utmost penalty. Yes, for every such passion is both cruel and tyrannical and insatiable, and never ceases to devour us every day. […]
1:6.s: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 4

1:6.t: We have spoken according to the history; let us pass on to the spiritual understanding, so that with the old men we may be able to hear: A nation has come up over the land of God, that is, the human soul. For all souls are God's; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son. And there comes up the nation of the princes of this world, and of darkness, and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, against whom we have our wrestling and struggle, of whom it is said: If the spirit of him who has power comes up over you, do not leave your place; the teeth of this nation are like the teeth of a lion, of whom the apostle Peter speaks: Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. And its molars are like a lion's whelp. By the lion's whelp understand either him who is lifted up against everything that is called God and religion, or certainly every perverse dogma. […]

For a nation has come up over my land, strong and without number; its teeth are like the teeth of a lion, and its molars like a lion's whelp. It has made my vine a desert, and has stripped the bark from my fig tree; stripping it, it has despoiled it, and cast it away; its branches have become white. LXX: For a nation has come up over the land, strong and without number; its teeth are the teeth of a lion, and its molars as of a lion's whelp. It has made my vine a destruction, and my figs a breaking; searching it has searched it, and cast it away; it has whitened its branches. The Jews think that in the days of Joel so countless a multitude of locusts came over Judea that they filled everything; and they left behind, I will not say the crops, but not even the bark and the branches of the vines and the trees, so that, all the greenness consumed, the whitening branches of the trees and the dry shoots of the vines remained. Whether this happened or not we cannot clearly affirm; […]

1:7.t: If, then, we give place to this nation to come up over us, at once it will make our vine a desert, the vine from which we used to make the wine that gladdens the heart of man; and it strips the bark from our figs, or breaks them, so that we may not have in us the sweetest gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that the holy man may not rest under our vine and fig tree, under which, when he is there, he will not fear the assault of the adversaries. Nor is it enough for this nation to destroy the vine and break the fig tree, unless, searching, it searches them, and kills whatever is living in them, so that, all the greenness consumed, white and dead twigs remain, and there is fulfilled in us: If they do these things in the green wood, what will they do in the dry?

1:8.t: Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth over the husband of your youth. LXX: Lament to me over a bride girded with haircloth, over her virgin husband. The husband of youth, or, as the Seventy translated, παρθενικὸς, whom people commonly call the virgin husband, because he was the first to take away the flower of virginity, is understood to be none other than God, who in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob betrothed to himself a virgin bride stained by no filth of idolatry. To her he speaks also through Jeremiah: Did you not call me lord, and father, and prince of your virginity?. Hence the Apostle also says to the believers: I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. As long as the bridegroom is with this bride, you cannot fast, nor lament, nor show by tears your longing for an absent bridegroom. But when the bridegroom has been taken away from her, she laments and wails, and girds herself with sackcloth and haircloth, and instead of a belt she is girded with a rope. […]

1:9.t: According to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy) this seems to us to be the sense: after the bride who had received the teaching of God has been separated from the bridegroom through her sins, and instead of garments of fine linen and linen has been girded with haircloth, that is, has taken on the dress of one who mourns, then the sacrifice will perish, of which it is written: A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit, and the libation of wine, which gladdens the heart of man, from the house of God, which is the Church, as the Apostle says to Timothy: That you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God. And the sacrifice and the libation will be taken away from the house of the Lord when, iniquity having multiplied, the love of many has grown cold; […]

The sacrifice and the libation have perished from the house of the Lord, and the priests, the ministers of the Lord, have mourned; the region is laid waste, the ground has mourned, because the wheat is devastated. The wine is confounded, the oil has languished, the farmers are confounded. The vinedressers have howled over the grain and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished; the vine is confounded and the fig tree has languished; the pomegranate and the palm and the apple tree, and all the trees of the field have dried up, because joy is confounded from the sons of men. LXX: The sacrifice and the libation have been taken away from the house of the Lord; mourn, you priests, ministers of the Lord, because the plains have been made desolate; let the land mourn, because the wheat is afflicted, the wine has dried up, the oil is diminished, the farmers have dried up; […]

1:11.t: Then the farmers will be confounded, when they see that in their possessions there springs up no wheat, by which men are nourished, and no barley, by which the irrational beasts of burden are sustained, and that the vine is confounded, of which it is written: Israel is a leafy vine, abundant fruit is in it; the Lord waiting for it to make grapes, and it made thorns. The fig tree too has languished, under which Nathanael was before he believed, and the pomegranate, to whose rind the cheeks of the bride are compared in the Song; and the palm, which, having lost its greenness, has dried up, of which it was once said: But the just man will flourish like the palm; and the apple tree, of which we read in the same Song: As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my kinsman among the sons. What need is there to run through all the trees, since all have dried up, and instead of joy and gladness grief and confusion have overwhelmed the sons of men?

1:13.t: Joel again summons us to wailing, and will have the ministers of the altar lament under the presence of famine: so far is he from allowing us to revel in the misfortunes of others: and, after sanctifying a fast, calling a solemn assembly, and gathering the old men, the children, and those of tender age, we ourselves must further haunt the temple in sackcloth and ashes, prostrated right humbly on the ground, because the field is wasted, and the meat-offering and the drink-offering is cut off from the house of the Lord, till we draw down mercy by our humiliation.

Gird yourselves and lament, you priests; howl, you ministers of the altar; go in, lie in sackcloth, you ministers of my God, because the sacrifice and the libation have perished from the house of your God; sanctify a fast, call an assembly, gather the old men, all the inhabitants of the earth, into the house of your God, and cry to the Lord. LXX: Gird yourselves and lament, you priests; bewail, you who minister at the altar; go in, sleep in sackcloths, you ministers of God, because the sacrifice and the libation have failed from the house of your God; sanctify a fast, proclaim a healing; gather the old men, all the inhabitants of the earth, into the house of your God, and cry to the Lord vehemently. Let him who is a holy priest, and eats the Passover of the Lord, be girded with the belt of chastity, and hear with the apostles: Let your loins be girded, and burning lamps in your hands. […]

1:14.t: Nor is it enough to weep, or to lament and take on the dress of one who mourns, unless they sanctify a fast and call an assembly. If every fast pleased God, he would never say: Sanctify a fast, and: I have not chosen such a fast, says the Lord. And in the Gospel those are condemned who disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to fast; and in the days, he says, of your fasts you strike with fists, and oppress the poor. Therefore he now says: Sanctify a fast. The Manichaean fasts, and many heretics, above all the Encratites, whose chief is Tatian; but this fast is worse than surfeit and drunkenness. And call an assembly, or a healing, so that through repentance we may heal our sins. For assembly, in the Hebrew one reads arasa, which Symmachus translated as synod, Aquila as day of gathering. Gather the old men, whose age, near to death and of riper judgment, takes up the fear and worship of God the more. […]

1:15.t: Ah, ah, ah for the day, because the day of the Lord is near, and like devastation from the mighty one it will come. LXX: Woe is me, woe is me, woe is me for the day, because the day of the Lord is near, and like misery from misery it will come. For what we have translated from the mighty one, and what in Hebrew is said saddai, which we have said several times is one of the ten names of God, the LXX translated misery, reading sud for saddai. So the voice of the priests and of the people crying to the Lord is brought in, so that they say three times: Woe is me. I believe it is because, through the sins they had committed, they had offended the holy Trinity. But the day of retribution for all sins is that of which all the prophets write, and above all Isaiah cries aloud: Behold, the incurable day of the Lord is coming, of fury and of wrath, to make the whole world a desert, and to destroy the sinners out of it. […]

1:16.t: Has not the nourishment perished before our eyes, from the house of our God, gladness and exultation? LXX: Before your eyes the nourishment has perished, from the house of our God gladness and joy. Before the eyes of sinners their nourishment perishes, when the crops already hoped for are taken out of their hands, and the locust forestalls the reaper, so that what in hope has been stored in the granaries the cankerworm and the blight consume. From those too who dwell in the Church, according to the quality of their merits, if they have sinned, the wheat of the spirit and the barley of the letter is taken away, so that they suffer hunger for the word of God. And when the nourishment has been taken away, it follows that joy and gladness are taken away from the house of God, so that those who before heard the Apostle saying: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice, afterward hear the Lord calling them to repentance: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.

1:17.t: The beasts of burden have rotted in their dung; the granaries are demolished, the storehouses are scattered, because the wheat is confounded; why has the animal groaned, have the herds of cattle lowed? Because there is no pasture for them, and even the flocks of small cattle have perished. LXX: The calves have leapt about in their stalls; the treasures are scattered, the winepresses are dug under, because the wheat has dried up; what shall we lay up for ourselves? The herds of oxen have wept, because there were no pastures for them, and the flocks of sheep have perished. After the nourishment had perished, and joy and gladness had been taken away from the house of God, the beasts of burden too rotted in their dung, or, according to the spiritual understanding, frolicked in their stalls and kicked against their creator, so that there was fulfilled what is written: If they are not filled, they will murmur. He rots in his dung whose god is his belly, and who says: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die; […]

What is a basket of dung, except the memory of sins? For the sins of the flesh are called dung. Hence it is also said through the prophet: "The beasts have rotted in their dung." For the beasts to rot in their dung is for carnal people to end their lives in the stench of luxury.

1:18.t: And when everything has dried up, then they will complain with a tearful voice and say: What shall we lay up for ourselves? And what follows according to the LXX: The herds of oxen have wept, because there are no pastures for them, compels us to take what has been said not of oxen and herds, but of those who because of their simplicity are called oxen and sheep. Of their pastures the Savior speaks: He will go in and go out, and will find pasture. But understand all these things under the metaphor of the caterpillar, the locust, the cankerworm and the blight: that when the crops had been taken away and laid waste, famine and pestilence took possession of everything.

The prophet says, "The beasts of burden have become putrid in their own dung." For beasts of burden to become putrid in their own dung means for all those who are materialistic to end their lives in the stench of dissipation. As often as we prove a materialistic heart for its sins, as often as we draw back to its memory the wrongs it has committed, it is as if we are turning a measure of dung onto a barren tree. It is to call to mind the evils it has done and grow fertile to the gift of compunction as if from the stench.
1:18.s: 40 Homilies on the Gospels, Homily X

1:19.t: To you, O Lord, I will cry, because fire has eaten the beautiful places of the desert, and the flame has set on fire all the trees of the region; and even the beasts of the field, like a garden bed thirsting for rain, have looked up to you, because the springs of waters have been dried up; and fire has devoured the beautiful places of the desert. LXX: To you, O Lord, I will cry, because fire has consumed the beautiful places of the desert, and the flame has set on fire all the trees of the field, and the beasts of burden of the plain have looked up to you, because the outflowings of waters have been dried up; and fire has devoured the beautiful places of the desert. As the prophet cries to the Lord, or the people through the prophet, because fire has eaten the beautiful places of the desert and the flame has set on fire all the trees of the region, the beasts and the beasts of burden of the field, or of the plain, have looked up to the Lord, like a little garden bed thirsting for rain. […]

2:1.t: I did not wish to divide a pericope joined and coherent in itself, lest what was one in sense should be plucked apart into different sections. Let us pass to the spiritual understanding, taking up each point again. The blast of trumpets and horns we read of not only in Leviticus and in the book of Numbers, in which it is commanded that Moses make two silver trumpets, with which, on the kalends, and in the seventh month on the first day of the month, and at the jubilee, and at the other festivals, and when they go forth to war, those who are bound to this office should sound; but it is also written that the walls of Jericho fell at the blast of the trumpets. And the Lord says that he will send his angel with the blast of a trumpet, and the Apostle proclaims that the resurrection of the dead takes place at the sound of the trumpet. And in the Apocalypse of John too we read that seven angels received a trumpet each, and as they sounded in order, the things came to pass which the Scripture describes. […]

Blow the trumpet in Zion; wail on my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the land be troubled, for the day of the Lord comes, for the day of darkness and gloom is near, a day of cloud and whirlwind; like the morning spread out over the mountains, a people many and strong; there has not been its like from the beginning, and after it there will not be, even to the years of generation and generation. Before its face a devouring fire, and behind it a burning flame; the land before it is like a garden of delight, and behind it the solitude of the desert, and there is none who escapes it; like the appearance of horses is their appearance, and like horsemen so shall they run; like the sound of four-horse chariots they shall leap upon the tops of the mountains; like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble, like a strong people prepared for battle; before its face the peoples shall be tormented; all faces shall be brought to a pot; like mighty men they shall run, like men of war they shall climb the wall; […]

The terror then of the Strict Inquest, which Zephaniah calls 'the Trumpet,' blessed Job designates 'thundering.' Which Joel also viewing saith, "Let all the inhabitants of the land be troubled; for the Day of the Lord cometh; for it is nigh at hand, a day of darkness and of gloominess, a day of cloud and whirlwind. For the Day of the Lord is great, and very terrible, and who shall sustain it?" But how incomprehensible and unimaginable that Greatness wherewith He shall come in His Second Manifesting, in some degree we estimate aright, if we consider with heedful reflection the weighty particulars of His first Advent. Surely that He might redeem us from death, the Lord came to die, and the impoverishment and punishments of our flesh He underwent in His own Body; Who before He came to the stock of the Cross, suffered Himself to be bound, to be spit on, to be mocked and to be beaten with blows on His cheek. […]
2:1.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book XVII, 54

2:2.t: It is a day of darkness and of distress, a day of cloud and whirlwind; for all things are full of punishments and torments. A people of angels, many and strong, will come, to render to each according to his works; and as the morning and the rising dawn first takes hold of the mountains, so judgment will begin from the lofty and the powerful, that the mighty may suffer torments mightily. There has not been its like from the beginning, and after it there will not be, even to the years of generation and generation. For all the evils which are contained in the ancient histories, and which befell men either by the flooding of the sea, or by the overflowing of rivers, or by pestilence, diseases, famine, beasts, the devastation of enemies, cannot be compared with these punishments which are to be rendered on the day of judgment.

Nor should you think it a feeble crowd: it is a people many and strong, and no other nation like it can be found, either in the past or in the future; whatever it touches it will consume like a ravenous flame, and will leave nothing whole behind it; like a garden and paradise of delight is all the land which it has not touched; like a solitude and a desert is whatever it has plundered, nor can anyone be found who escapes its hands.

2:3.t: Before the face of this people, which is strong and many, there will be a devouring, or consuming, fire, to consume all the hay, wood and stubble in us. Whence it is also said of God: God is a consuming fire, and behind him a burning flame; so that he leaves nothing without punishment. Whomever this people has not touched, and in whom it has not found material for burning, will be likened to the garden of God and to the paradise of delight, which in Hebrew is called Eden. But if it burns anyone, it will reduce him like a solitude to ashes and embers, nor is there anyone who can escape its fury; its cruel appearance will have the likeness of snorting horses; and so they will run about to torment those whom they have received into their power, like horsemen flying hither and thither; terrible will be their sound, like that of four-horse chariots running down a slope; and they will leap upon the tops of the mountains, desiring to torment all the lofty and those set on the summit of the Church. […]

2:4.t: Their appearance is like that of fierce horses, and like horsemen they will run about hither and thither. Not that the Babylonians are compared to horsemen, but that the locusts, by a figure for the enemies, are said to run about hither and thither like horsemen: As the sound, he says, of four-horse chariots and of carts, so will be the sound of the locusts. They will leap upon the tops of the mountains, so as to climb all the lofty places; and as a flame quickly consumes stubble, so the sound and the terror of their voice will lay waste all things. And what he adds: Like a strong people prepared for battle, he refers again to the locusts, so that he seems to speak not as of enemies but as of locusts; and yet while we read of locusts, let us think of the Babylonians.

2:6.t: So great will the terror be that all the nations round about will shudder both in mind and in body, or rather will be tormented; and from the greatness of their dread the faces of all will be turned into the likeness of a pot, which, burned by the fire, shows the blackness and soot of a foul appearance.
So great will be the fear of all, so great the consciousness of sins, that no one will shine or have the splendor of joy, but like a scorched pot his face will be turned into darkness.

2:7.t: They will run about, he says, like mighty men, no doubt the locusts: and like men of war they shall climb the wall, so that the height of the walls cannot check the onset of the strong, and they enter by no means through the gates, but over the walls: Each one shall walk in his own ways, and they shall not turn aside from their paths. This we saw lately in this province. For when the hosts of locusts came and filled the air which is between heaven and earth, they flew in such order, by the disposition of God who commanded them, that, like the little tesserae which are fixed in pavements by the hand of the craftsman, they kept their place, and did not swerve even by a point and, so to speak, by a nail's breadth, to another. And to make the metaphor plain, and through the windows, he says, they shall fall, and shall not be destroyed. For nothing is impassable to locusts, since they penetrate fields, and crops, and trees, and cities, and houses, and the secret places of bedchambers. […]

They will climb the wall and every fortification; and fulfilling the work enjoined on them, they will not turn aside to another part, but will cling to the punishments of the wretched, nor will they be sated with their torments, but each will carry out the punishments entrusted to him against sinners.

2:8.t: Moreover they will enter through the windows, or will fall, or, weighed down with their arms, will walk, and upon their javelins will fall those whom they have received to be consumed. These are the windows of which Jeremiah also says: Death has entered through our windows; for the enemies desire to enter through all our senses, and to take the city of a good conscience, and to run about through our fortifications, and to destroy the houses which we have built for ourselves by good works. And they do all things entering through the windows like a thief, for they do not enter openly, that they may shoot in the dark at the upright of heart.

2:9.t: And he keeps up the narration he has begun, so as to say that they enter the city, run about on the walls, climb up the houses, and enter through the windows like thieves; not that those who are victors have the fear of thieves, but as thieves are wont to enter through windows and to steal in secret, so they, the doors being shut, lest there be any delay, will burst in through the windows with complete boldness.

2:10.t: What, then, is the vanity, and what the lie? The holy apostle of the Lord, reprehending the Greeks, will show thee: "Because that, when they knew God, they glorified Him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and changed the glory of God into the likeness of corruptible man, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator." And verily this is the God who "in the beginning made the heaven and the earth." But you do not know God, and worship the heaven, and how shall you escape the guilt of impiety? Hear again the prophet speaking: "The sun, shall suffer eclipse, and the heaven be darkened; but the Almighty shall shine for ever: while the powers of the heavens shall be shaken, and the heavens stretched out and drawn together shall be rolled as a parchment-skin (for these are the prophetic expressions), and the earth shall flee away from before the face of the Lord."

Before the face of locusts of this kind the earth trembled, and the heavens were moved, which we should take as said hyperbolically: not that the force of locusts or of enemies is so great that it could move the heavens and shake the earth, but that to those who suffer adversity, from the greatness of their terror, the heaven seems to fall and the earth to heave. Finally, because of the multitude of locusts covering the sky, the sun and the moon will be turned into darkness, and the stars will withdraw their splendor, while the cloud of locusts placed in between does not let the light reach the earth.

Before the face of this people, which is many and strong, the earth trembled, and the heavens were moved. For heaven and earth shall pass away, but the word of the Lord abides forever. Moreover the sun and the moon will not be able to look upon such great punishments of the wretched, and they will mourn, not having the righteousness of their office, and instead of clear light they will be covered with dreadful darkness; the stars too will withdraw their brightness, while even those who are holy will not see the presence of the Lord without dread.

2:11.t: The Lord also will give his voice before the face of so powerful an army, for his camps are many, and the greatness of his power is shown even in small creatures. And these many and innumerable camps are exceedingly strong, and doing his word. By this saying it is shown that the Babylonians will come by the will of God, and will obey his command. Great is, he says, the day of the Lord, in which Jerusalem is to be taken, and very terrible; and no one will be able to endure it, and to escape the necessity of captivity or of death.

In all these things the Lord will give his voice before the face of his army. For as the Babylonians, punishing Jerusalem, are called the army of God, so the most wicked angels, of whom it is written: Fury and wrath and distress, a sending by most wicked angels, are called the army of God and are named his camps, while they do the will of the Lord. Great is the day of the Lord and terrible, of which it is written elsewhere: Why do you desire the day of the Lord? And this is darkness, and not light; and very terrible; and hardly anyone, or no one, will be able to endure it without offering in himself material for its raging.

2:12.t: I, the messenger of repentance, say unto you, Fear not the devil; for I was sent to be with you who repent with all your heart, and to make you strong in faith. Trust God, then, ye who on account of your sins have despaired of life, and who add to your sins and weigh down your life; for if ye return to the Lord with all your heart, and practise righteousness the rest of your days, and serve Him according to His will, He will heal your former sins, and you will have power to hold sway over the works of the devil.

Now therefore says the Lord: Turn to me with your whole heart, in fasting, and in weeping and in mourning; and rend your hearts, and not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, for he is kind and merciful, patient and of much mercy, and placable over evil; who knows if he will turn and pardon, and leave behind him a blessing, sacrifice and libation to the Lord our God? LXX: And now says the Lord our God: Turn to me from your whole heart, in fasting, and in weeping and in mourning; and rend your hearts, and not your garments; and turn to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and compassionate, patient and of much mercy, and repenting over evils; who knows if he will return and repent, and leave behind him a blessing, sacrifice and libation to the Lord our God? The preceding section, from the place where it is written: Blow the trumpet in Zion, wail on my holy mountain; […]

Of what avail, dearly-beloved, are religious fasts in winning the mercy of God, and in renewing the fortunes of human frailty, we know from the statements of the holy Prophets, who proclaim that justice of God, Whose vengeance the people of Israel had again and again incurred through their iniquities, cannot be appeased save by fasting. Thus it is that the Prophet Joel warns them, saying, “thus saith the Lord your God, turn ye to Me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning, and rend your hearts and not your garments, and turn ye to the Lord your God, for He is merciful and patient, and of great kindness, and very merciful,” and again, “sanctify a fast, proclaim a healing, assemble the people, sanctify the church.” And this exhortation must in our days also be obeyed, because these healing remedies must of necessity be proclaimed by us too, in order that in the observance of the ancient sanctification Christian devotion may gain what Jewish transgression lost.

2:13.t: Let each one confess his sin, I beseech you, brethren, while he who has sinned is still in this world, while his confession can be admitted, while the satisfaction and remission effected through the priest is pleasing with the Lord. Let us turn to the Lord with our whole mind, and, expressing repentance for our sin with true grief, let us implore God's mercy. Let the soul prostrate itself before him; let sorrow give satisfaction to him; let our every hope rest upon him. He himself tells how we ought to ask. He says, "Return to me with all your hearts, in fasting and in weeping, and in mourning, and rend your hearts, not your garments." Let us return to the Lord with a whole heart; let us placate his wrath and displeasure by fastings, weepings and mournings, as he himself admonishes.

And since it is the custom that in sad and adverse things you rend your clothes, which the high priest too is recorded in the Gospel to have done, to aggravate the charge against the Lord the Savior; and which we read that Paul and Barnabas did on hearing words of blasphemy. Therefore I command you by no means to rend your garments, but your hearts, which are full of sins, and which, like wineskins, unless they have been rent, will burst of themselves. And when you have done this, return to the Lord your God, whom your former sins had made a stranger to you; and do not despair of pardon because of the greatness of your crimes, for great mercy will blot out great sins. For he is kind and merciful, preferring the repentance of sinners to their death, patient and great in mercy, one who does not imitate human impatience, but waits a long time for our repentance; […]

Theodore: Sometimes holy Scripture is wont by an improper use of terms to use "evils "for "affliction;" not that these are properly and in their nature evils, but because they are imagined to be evils by those on whom they are brought for their good. For when divine judgment is reasoning with men it must speak with the language and feelings of men. For when a doctor for the sake of health with good reason either cuts or cauterizes those who are suffering from the inflammation of ulcers, it is considered an evil by those who have to bear it. Nor are the spur and the whip pleasant to a restive horse. Moreover all chastisement seems at the moment to be a bitter thing to those who are chastised, as the Apostle says: "Now all chastisement for the present indeed seemeth not to bring with it joy but sorrow; […]

2:14.t: Let us anticipate His anger by confession; let us desire to see Him appeased, after He was wroth. Who knoweth, he says, if He will turn and repent, and leave a blessing behind Him? This I know certainly, I the sponsor of the loving-kindness of God. And when He has laid aside that which is unnatural to Him, His anger, He will betake Himself to that which is natural, His mercy. To the one He is forced by us, to the other He is inclined. And if He is forced to strike, surely He will refrain, according to His Nature. Only let us have mercy on ourselves, and open a road for our Father's righteous affections.

And likewise, because he had said above, kind and merciful, patient and great in mercy, and placable, or repenting over evils, lest perhaps the greatness of his clemency should make us careless, he adds in the person of the prophet and says: Who knows if he will turn and pardon, and leave behind him a blessing? I, he says, exhort to repentance, which is my part, and I know that God is ineffably merciful, as David says: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity. But because we cannot know the depth of the riches and of the wisdom and knowledge of God, I temper my statement, and I wish rather than presume, saying: Who knows if he will turn and pardon? When he says who, it is to be understood as either impossible or difficult: Sacrifice and libation to the Lord our God; so that after he has given the blessing and has forgiven us our sins, we may be able to offer victims to God.

2:15.t: For since, as I before said, there are divers proclamations, listen, as in a figure, to the prophet blowing the trumpet; and further, having turned to the truth, be ready for the announcement of the trumpet, for he saith, ‘Blow ye the trumpet in Sion: sanctify a fast.’ This is a warning trumpet, and commands with great earnestness, that when we fast, we should hallow the fast. For not all those who call upon God, hallow God, since there are some who defile Him; yet not Him—that is impossible—but their own mind concerning Him; for He is holy, and has pleasure in the saints. And therefore the blessed Paul accuses those who dishonour God; ‘Transgressors of the law dishonour God.’ So then, to make a separation from those who pollute the fast, he saith here, ‘sanctify a fast.’ For many, crowding to the fast, pollute themselves in the thoughts of their hearts, sometimes by doing evil against their brethren, sometimes by daring to defraud. […]

Sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly, as blessed Joel with us charges you: gather the elders, and the babes that suck the breasts, whose tender age wins our pity, and is specially worthy of the loving-kindness of God. I know also what he enjoins both upon me, the minister of God, and upon you, who have been thought worthy of the same honour, that we should enter His house in sackcloth and lament night and day between the porch and the altar, in piteous array, and with more piteous voices, crying aloud without ceasing on behalf of ourselves and the people, sparing nothing, either toil or word, which may propitiate God: saying "Spare, O Lord, Thy people, and give not Thine heritage to reproach," and the rest of the prayer; surpassing the people in our sense of the affliction as much as in our rank, instructing them in our own persons in compunction and correction of wickedness, and in the consequent long-suffering of God, and cessation of the scourge.

Blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call an assembly, gather the people, sanctify the Church, assemble the old men, gather the little ones and those that suck the breasts. Let the bridegroom go forth from his bed and the bride from her bridal chamber. Between the vestibule and the altar the priests, the ministers of the Lord, shall weep, and shall say: Spare, O Lord, your people, and do not give your inheritance to reproach, that the nations should rule over them. Why do they say among the peoples: Where is their God? LXX: Sound the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, proclaim a healing, gather the people, sanctify the Church, choose the old men; gather the little ones and those that suck the breasts, let the bridegroom go forth from his bed, and the bride from her bridal chamber. […]

2:17.t: And as to what follows: Between the vestibule and the altar the priests shall weep, for vestibule the LXX translated base; Symmachus προπύλον (gateway); Aquila πρόδομον (front hall); Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, ulam, which we can call the space before the doors of the temple, and the portico. And note what he commands the priests who are ministers of the Lord: that they weep between the temple and the altar, and say with the Apostle: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn? and: To weep with those who weep. And the place fit for repentance and confession is the temple and the altar; and he teaches what the priests ought to say, or rather how they ought to entreat the Lord: Spare, O Lord, your people, which, when it sinned, was called not your people; now, after it has withdrawn from its vices, is called your people. And do not give your inheritance to reproach, that the nations should rule over them. The riddle that lay hidden is laid open. […]

2:18.t: The Lord was jealous for his land, and spared his people; and the Lord answered and said to his people: Behold, I will send you grain and wine and oil, and you shall be filled with it, and I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations; and him who is from the north I will put far from you, and I will drive him into a land pathless and desert; his face toward the eastern sea, and his hinder part toward the last sea, and his stench shall go up, and his rottenness shall go up, because he has acted proudly. LXX: And the Lord was jealous for his land, and spared his people, and the Lord answered, and said to his people: Behold, I will send you grain and wine and oil, and you shall be filled with them, and I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations, and him who is from the north I will drive back from you, and I will lead him out into a land which is without water, and I will destroy his face into the first sea, and his hinder parts into the last sea; […]

But according to tropology, every soul is the land of the Lord, in which the householder sows his seed; and when it has produced tares instead of wheat, that is, wild oats and darnel, and has offended its Lord, and afterwards has done penance, and has said in mourning: Spare, O Lord, your people, the Lord is jealous for his land, and will spare it, which he had long despised, and deigns to address it and says: I will send you grain, of which it is written: Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears many fruits and wine which gladdens the heart of man, and oil which makes the face cheerful, so that the old sadness of sins may be tempered by the gladness of grain and wine and oil, that is, of the virtues; and they will have such an abundance of all good things that they will be filled and sated with them. […]

2:20.t: And the Assyrian and Chaldean, who is from the north, I will put far from you, of whom it is written above: A people many and strong, before its face a devouring fire, and behind it a burning flame; like the appearance of horses is their appearance. And I will drive him, he says, into a land of solitude; and his front parts will fall into the eastern sea, and his hinder parts into the last sea, and his stench will go up, that is, the stench of him who is from the north, and his rottenness, because he acted proudly. I have often pointed out that under the figure of locusts is described the onset of the Chaldeans, by which Judea was laid waste. Accordingly he keeps the metaphor in what remains, and speaks according to the situation of the province, so that he seems to speak not of enemies but of locusts. […]

Him also who is from the north — of whom Jeremiah speaks: From the north evils shall blaze up upon all the inhabitants of the land; of whom Solomon also writes: The north wind is a most harsh wind —; I will put him far from you, he says, and I will drive him into a land pathless and desert, which has no knowledge of God, in which the Holy Spirit does not dwell. And his face will be in the first sea and in the last sea, in those who have opened to him the door of sins, and with whom they have remained to the last moment of life; and his stench and rottenness goes up even upon those who promise great things to themselves, and fall through pride, because human frailty is never safe, and the more we grow in virtues, the more we ought to fear lest we fall from the heights. According to the letter, it is the south wind rather than the north wind that usually brings swarms of locusts, that is, they come not from the cold but from the heat. […]

2:21.t: Let us pass to the order of the spiritual understanding: Do not fear, O land, nay rather take courage and be glad, you who before had lost the Lord's seed by your dryness, because the Lord has magnified himself so as to show mercy to you, to such a degree that even the cattle of the region and of the desert solitude were filled with glad fallow lands, and the tree of the cross bore its fruit, and the most sweet gifts of the Holy Spirit bestowed their bounty on all.

Do not fear, O land: exult and be glad, for the Lord has magnified himself in acting; do not fear, animals of the region, for the beautiful places of the desert have sprouted, for the tree has borne its fruit, the fig tree and the vine have given their power; and sons of Zion: exult and be glad in the Lord your God, for he has given you a teacher of righteousness, and he will make the morning rain come down to you, and the late rain in the beginning; and the threshing floors shall be filled with grain, and the presses shall overflow with wine and oil, and I will restore to you the years which the locust, the cankerworm, and the blight, and the caterpillar have eaten. My great strength which I sent among you; and you shall eat, feeding, and be filled, and you shall praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders with you, and my people shall not be confounded for evermore; […]

2:23.t: You too, whom after repentance I rightly call sons of Zion and of the Church, be glad and rejoice, because God the Father has given you a teacher of righteousness, or has granted you nourishment of righteousness, and has made the early and late rains come down to you. The seasonable rain is when we first receive doctrine, the late rain when we receive the fruits of our labor, and come to the perfect knowledge of the holy Scriptures. The early and the late rain can also be taken as the Old and the New Testament.

He speaks also especially to the sons of Zion, that they should exult and rejoice, not in any trifling thing, but in the Lord their God, who has given them the nourishment of righteousness, and, as the Seventy translated, and the early and the late rain, so that they may eat and be glad, and praise the name of the Lord their God, who has done wonders with them, and may by no means be confounded; and may know that the Lord God of Israel dwells in their midst, and besides him there is no other, because the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, and his people will not be confounded forever. These things, according to the letter, since they were promised by the Lord, we believe to have come to pass, and the past barrenness to have been made up by new crops, so that whatever the locust, the cankerworm, and the blight, and the caterpillar had consumed, τροπικῶς (figuratively), was replenished in the following years.

2:24.t: And not only, he says, has he given this, but he has made you abound in new crops of virtues, and be filled and inebriated with grain, wine and oil of which we have often spoken.

2:25.t: We ask why the caterpillar was called the strength, or the power, of the Lord, and not only power, but great power? As the might of God was shown in the plagues of Egypt through small creatures, and especially the gnats, which are midges so small that they can scarcely be seen by the eyes, so now too in a small and slow little worm, which can scarcely move, and is crushed by a light touch, the might of God and human frailty are shown. Not that God cannot, at his nod and by the majesty of his might, overturn the earth, and cover all things with a flood, or burn them up with lightning, but through small things and, so to speak, mere points of bodies, he shows human frailty. Hence we are also accustomed to answer Marcion and the other heretics who tear the Old Testament to pieces, that God made fleas and midges and bugs, and creatures of this kind, for this reason, to show the frailty and weakness of our flesh, which is so much nothing that it is wounded by these things that are small. […]

And as for the years which you had lost through the perturbations that formerly reigned in you, when the locust, the cankerworm, the blight and the caterpillar had consumed your works. God did not suffer them to perish for you.

2:26.t: Then you will eat the fruits of righteousness, and be filled, and praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders with you. But if after repentance God promises such plenty of all things, what will Novatus answer, who denies repentance, and that sinners can be restored to their former state, if they do works worthy of repentance? For God receives the penitent to such a degree that he calls them his people, and declares that they are by no means to be confounded, and promises that he will dwell in their midst, and that they will no longer have another God, but will trust with their whole mind in him who abides in them forever.

2:28.t: I have already said, and do again say, that it had been prophesied that this would be done by Him after His ascension to heaven. It is accordingly said, 'He ascended on high, He led captivity captive, He gave gifts unto the sons of men.' And again, in another prophecy it is said: 'And it shall come to pass after this, I will pour out My Spirit on all flesh, and on My servants, and on My handmaids, and they shall prophesy.'

You hold to the Scriptures in which the flesh is disparaged; receive also those in which it is ennobled. You read whatever passage abases it. Now direct your eyes also to that which elevates it. "All flesh is grass." Well, but Isaiah was not content to say only this; he also declared, "All flesh shall see the salvation of God." Then notice what God says in Genesis: "My spirit shall not remain among these men, because they are flesh"; but then he is also heard saying by Joel, "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh." Even the apostle ought not to be known for any one statement in which he is inclined to reproach the flesh. Admittedly he says that "in his flesh dwells no good thing" and "they who are in the flesh cannot please God," because "the flesh lusts against the Spirit." Yet in these and similar assertions that he makes, it is not the substance of the flesh, but its actions, which are censured. […]
2:28.s: ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 10

2:28.t: We declare, then, that dreams are inflicted on us mainly by demons, although they sometimes turn out true and favorable to us. When, however, with the deliberate aim after evil, of which we have just spoken, they assume a flattering and captivating style, they show themselves proportionately vain, and deceitful, and obscure, and wanton, and impure. And no wonder that the images partake of the character of the realities. But from God—who has promised, indeed, "to pour out the grace of the Holy Spirit upon all flesh, and has ordained that his servants and his handmaids should see visions as well as utter prophecies"—must all those visions be regarded as emanating. [Those visions] may be compared with the actual grace of God, as being honest, holy, prophetic, inspired, instructive, inviting to virtue, the bountiful nature of which causes them to overflow even to the profane, since God, with grand impartiality, "sends his showers and sunshine on the just and on the unjust."

Now we are of the opinion that every rational creature, without any distinction, receives a share of him in the same way as of the wisdom and of the word of God. I observe, however, that the chief advent of the Holy Spirit is declared to people after the ascension of Christ into heaven, rather than before his coming into the world. For before that, it was on the prophets alone, and on a few individuals, if there happened to be among the people any deserving, that the gift of the Holy Spirit was conferred. But after the advent of the Savior, it is written that the prediction of the prophet Joel was fulfilled: "In the last days it shall come to pass, and I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy," which is similar to the well-known statement, "All nations shall serve him." By the grace, then, of the Holy Spirit, along with numerous other results, this most glorious consequence is clearly demonstrated. […]

These things being thus demonstrated, it is superfluous to touch upon the other points, or to enter upon any discussion relating to them, since the body in which the Word was is not coessential with the Godhead, but was truly born of Mary, while the Word Himself was not changed into bones and flesh, but came in the flesh. For what John said, ‘The Word was made flesh,’ has this meaning, as we may see by a similar passage; for it is written in Paul: ‘Christ has become a curse for us.’ And just as He has not Himself become a curse, but is said to have done so because He took upon Him the curse on our behalf, so also He has become flesh not by being changed into flesh, but because He assumed on our behalf living flesh, and has become Man. For to say ‘the Word became flesh,’ is equivalent to saying ‘the Word has become man;’ according to what is said in Joel: ‘I will pour forth of My Spirit upon all flesh;’ for the promise did not extend to the irrational animals, but is for men, on whose account the Lord is become Man. […]

And He was promised by the mouth of Joel first, who said, And it shall be in the last days that I will pour out of My Spirit upon all flesh (that is, upon all that believe), and upon your sons and upon your daughters, and the rest; and then afterwards by Jesus, being glorified by Him, and giving back glory to Him, as He was glorified by and glorified the Father. And how abundant was this Promise. He shall abide for ever, and shall remain with you, whether now with those who in the sphere of time are worthy, or hereafter with those who are counted worthy of that world, when we have kept Him altogether by our life here, and not rejected Him in so far as we sin.

But of what creature can it be said that it fills all things, as is written of the Holy Spirit: "I will pour My Spirit upon all flesh." This cannot be said of an Angel. Lastly, Gabriel himself, when sent to Mary, said: "Hail, full of grace," plainly declaring the grace of the Spirit which was in her, because the Holy Spirit had come upon her, and she was about to have her womb full of grace with the heavenly Word.

But that the Spirit is the Arbiter of the Divine Counsel, you may know even from this. For when above we showed that the Holy Spirit was the Lord of baptism, and read that baptism is the counsel of God, as you read, "But the Pharisees despised the counsel of God, not being baptized of Him," it is quite clear that as there can be no baptism without the Spirit, so, too, the counsel of God is not without the Spirit. And that we may know more completely that the Spirit is Power, we ought to know that He was promised when the Lord said: "I will pour out of My Spirit upon all flesh." He, then, Who was promised to us is Himself Power, as in the Gospel the same Son of God declared when He said: "And I will send the promise of the Father upon you, but do you remain in the city until ye be endued with power from on high."

Hence we learn that on unessential points one must not spend many words. And besides, the sequel is enough to bear him out on this point: so now the discourse is for all in common. "But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel, And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith the Lord God." Nowhere as yet the name of Christ, nor His promises but the promise is that of the Father.... "And I will pour out of My Spirit upon all flesh." He offers even to them excellent hopes, if they would have them. And so far, he does not leave it to be regarded as the exclusive advantage of himself and his company; which would have made them be looked upon with an evil eye; thus cutting off all envious feeling. "And your sons shall prophesy." And yet, he says, not yours this achievement, this distinction; the gift has passed over to your children. Himself and his company he calls their sons, and those whom he is addressing he calls his and their fathers. […]
2:28.s: Homily on the Acts of the Apostles 5

2:28.t: But all flesh, upon which the Lord promises that he will pour out of his spirit, is that of which Isaiah speaks: And all flesh shall see the salvation of God. Therefore the salvation of God cannot be seen unless the Holy Spirit is poured out. And whoever says that he believes in Christ, not believing in the Holy Spirit, will not have the eyes of perfect faith. Hence also in the Acts of the Apostles, those who had been baptized with the baptism of John into him who was to come, that is, in the name of the Lord Jesus, because they answered Paul when he asked them: But we do not even know whether there is a Holy Spirit, are baptized again; or rather they receive true baptism, because without the Holy Spirit and the mystery of the Trinity, whatever is received in one or another person is imperfect. Nor indeed will everyone who has received the Holy Spirit at once have spiritual grace as well, but through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit they will obtain diverse graces. […]

The word of outpouring too, which in Hebrew is called esphoch, and which all have translated alike, shows the bounty of the gift, in that the gifts of the Holy Spirit have come down by no means upon a few prophets — as used to happen in the Old Testament —, but upon all who believe in the name of the Savior; by no means upon this one and that one, but upon all flesh. For there is no distinction of Jew and Greek, slave and free, man and woman, for we are all one in Christ. Hence also Agabus prophesied at Caesarea, and in Antioch there were very many prophets; and the Apostle commands that if, while one is prophesying, something has been revealed to another, the first should be silent. And we read that the four daughters of Philip the evangelist prophesied. Old men too saw dreams, when Paul, already an old man, heard a man of Macedonia saying to him: Come over to Macedonia and help us. […]

And it shall be after these things, I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions; moreover upon my servants and my handmaids in those days I will pour out my spirit, and I will give wonders in heaven and on earth, blood, and fire, and vapors of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and dreadful day of the Lord comes. And it shall be, everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. LXX: And it shall be after these things, I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions; and upon my servants and upon my handmaids in those days I will pour out of my spirit, and I will give wonders in heaven, and upon the earth blood, fire and vapor of smoke. […]

This passage is most difficult and admits a manifold explanation. Let us, then, under tropology, refer all that has been said to those times to which the apostles Peter and Paul referred it, that is, when the Lord suffered and rose again. For it cannot be that we understand the earlier things of the time of the passion, and those that follow of the day of judgment, especially since there follows: For behold, in those days, and at that time, and this little verse, connecting what comes after with what precedes, says that all things were accomplished at one time.

This is Joel the second in order who was privileged to prophesy concerning the mystery of the Lord Christ, for he speaks thus (chap. ii, 28-32): And it shall come to pass afterward that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions; and also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit. And I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth, blood and fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord come. And it shall come to pass that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered—a passage which the blessed Peter mentions in the Acts of the Apostles as having been fulfilled when the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles occurred on the day of Pentecost.

2:30.t: Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be moved. And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven, and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn (24, 29—30ᵃ). Since we consider that greater themes here come under discussion than lie within the grasp of human understanding — even of those who have advanced in wisdom far beyond others — let us come and examine the passage: first inquiring into those things which can readily be admitted for an exposition of the Gospel text, as though the Lord Himself were prophesying in it; and afterward we shall look for what the truth of these words may be according to those who judge that there is something deeper and more subtle in the words, keeping to the sequence of the moral traditions in these matters as well, in the same manner as above. […]

Then the Lord will give wonders in heaven and on earth: in heaven, because the sun was turned into darkness and the moon into blood; on earth, because the earth trembled with so violent and unusual a motion that the tombs were opened and the rocks split. And as to his saying blood and vapors, or vapor of smoke, that blood is the one of which we read in the psalms: That your foot may be dipped in blood. And in Isaiah: How red are your garments. And the blood which, when the Savior's side was pierced, the Roman soldier shed mixed with water. And the fire of the Holy Spirit, which came down from heaven, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: There appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it sat upon each of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit; and they began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them to speak. This is the fire which the Lord came to send upon the earth, and which, before he suffered, he longed to burn in his disciples. […]

2:31.t: He describes all these things as to come before the great and dreadful day of the Lord comes. But the great and dreadful day of the Lord is to be believed to be either that of the resurrection, or certainly, many ages later, the day of judgment, which is truly great and dreadful. But since there follows: And it shall be, everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved, and the apostle Paul refers this to the time of the Lord's passion, it is rather to be understood of the day of the resurrection. For he says, writing to the Romans: There is no distinction of Jew and Greek. For the same one is Lord of all: rich toward all who call upon him. For everyone, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved. How then shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent. […]

2:32.t: Yet some one may say that it is written: “Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved,” so that the mere calling upon the name of the Lord is enough to save him that calls. Let him rather hearken to the apostle who says: “How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” And if thou believest, hear the Lord Who says: “Not every one that saith unto me Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” For indeed when a man does the will of God, but not as God wills, nor with a disposition of love towards God, his zeal for good works is fruitless, according to the will of our Lord Jesus Christ, Who says: “This they do that they may be seen of men; verily I say unto you, they have received their reward.” Wherefore Paul was taught to say: “And if I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but have not love, it profiteth me nothing.”

Return, then, to the Church, those of you who have wickedly separated yourselves. For He promises forgiveness to all who are converted, since it is written: "Whosoever shall call on the Name of the Lord shall be saved." And lastly, the Jewish people who said of the Lord Jesus, "He hath a devil," and "He casteth out devils through Beelzebub," and who crucified the Lord Jesus, are, by the preaching of Peter, called to baptism, that they may put away the guilt of so great a wickedness.

For in mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be salvation, as the Lord has said; and in the remnant whom the Lord shall call. LXX: For in mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be he who has been saved? As the Lord has said, and announcing those whom the Lord called. In the place where we have put salvation, or the one saved, and in the Hebrew is written phaleta, Symmachus translated, he who has fled. And again, where we said, in the remnant, and the LXX translated, announcing, in the Hebrew is read saridim, which the Jews think is the name of a place. After, therefore, the great and dreadful day of the Lord came, and whoever after the Lord's resurrection called upon his name was made safe, everyone who was on mount Zion and in Jerusalem was saved; for out of Zion went forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, of which it is written: It cannot be that a prophet perish outside Jerusalem. […]

3:1.t: For behold, in those days and at that time, when I shall turn back the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all the nations, and I will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and I will plead with them there over my people and my inheritance Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations; and they have divided my land, and over my people they have cast the lot; and they have put a boy in a brothel, and sold a girl for wine, that they might drink. LXX: For behold, I, in those days and at that time, when I shall turn back the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, will gather all the nations, and I will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and I will plead with them there for my people and my inheritance Israel, who have been scattered among the Gentiles; and they have divided my land, and over my people they have cast lots; and they have put a boy in a brothel, and they were selling girls for wine, and they were drinking. […]

All of which the Jews recall to have been fulfilled according to the letter in the times of Vespasian and Titus, and above all of Hadrian. But if we wish to refer what is written to the day of judgment, we say that everyone who is saved is saved in the Church, or in the heavenly Jerusalem. And after the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem has been turned back, then all are to be gathered and brought down into the valley of Jehoshaphat; and there the Lord will plead with those who have persecuted his people, and have divided among themselves the inheritance of the Lord, and have scattered them among the nations, and have cast the lot over his land. And these things we ought to take not only of the heretics, who have divided the people of God among themselves and make them Gentiles, but also of every harsh and proud teacher, who under the name of teaching and of the priesthood lord it over those allotted to them and oppress those who are subject to them. […]

3:3.t: Under these names the people of God was once divided; and the adverse nations, that is, the princes of this world and the rulers of darkness, not only divided the people of God among themselves, but put boys into the brothel, to compel them to change their male nature, of whom the Apostle speaks: For this reason God gave them up to passions of disgrace; for their women exchanged the natural use for that use which is against nature. And likewise the males also, having left the natural use of the woman, were inflamed in their desire toward one another, males working shamefulness on males, and receiving in themselves the recompense of their error which was due. And not content to have done this, they sold a girl for wine, that they might drink, and put gluttony before lust.

3:4.t: But what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon, and all the border of the Philistines? Will you render vengeance to me? And if you avenge yourselves against me, quickly, swiftly I will return your recompense upon your head. For you have taken my silver and my gold, and my desirable things, and the most beautiful you have carried into your shrines; and the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem you have sold to the sons of the Greeks, that you might remove them far from their borders. LXX: What have I to do with you, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of the foreigners? Are you rendering me retribution, or do you keep anger in your heart against me? — for this is what μνησικακείτε means in Greek —. Swiftly and quickly I will return your retribution upon your heads, because you have taken my silver and my gold, and my choice and best things you have carried into your temples, and the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem you have sold to the sons of the Greeks, that you might cast them out of their borders. […]

For Galilee, in the Hebrew is written Galiloth, which Aquila translated Θῖνας, Symmachus borders; and Θῖνας, that is, mounds of sand, let us refer to the shores of Palestine, not to a Galilee of the Philistines, which does not exist at all.

They refer this against Tyre and Sidon so as to maintain that the vengeance for the blood of Christ and the overthrow of Jerusalem, which happened by the judgment of God, happened of itself. But let us, following the tropology we have begun, interpret Tyre and Sidon and the Philistines as those who hem in and afflict and persecute the people of God — for this is what Tyre sounds in our language —, and hunt him to death, which the name of Sidon indicates, and, drinking blood, fall down, or wallow in the mire, which is what the Philistines and Galilee signify. Swiftly and quickly the Lord will repay them what they deserve, because they have persecuted him. And his silver and gold, namely the words of the Scriptures, and the νοήματα, that is, the meanings, and everything that was beautiful in the Church, they have made the slaves of their errors. […]

3:5.t: I will repay you, he says, what you have done to my people, because you have taken my silver and gold, that is, the vessels of the temple, and whatever was most precious and most splendid in it, the golden lampstand and the golden table of the showbread, and the two golden Cherubim, and the mercy seat, and the golden bowls and censers, and have consecrated them to your idols. But history relates that it was rather the Chaldeans who did these things, who placed the vessels of the temple of the Lord in the temple of Bel, from which Belshazzar afterward drinks in the bowls, and at once his kingdom is transferred to the Medes and Persians. But since these things are said to be going to happen after the great and terrible day of the Lord, which the apostles interpret of the resurrection of the Lord, and the Hebrews defer to the future time of judgment, it is rather to be understood of the Romans; […]

3:6.t: At that time the sons of Judah and Jerusalem — by no means Israel and the ten tribes, which to this day dwell in the cities and mountains of the Medes —, were sold to the sons of the Greeks, to be banished from their borders, and the whole world was filled with the Jewish captivity.

3:7.t: The Jews, then, promise themselves, or rather dream, that in the last time they will be gathered by the Lord and brought back to Jerusalem. And not content with this happiness, they assert that God himself will deliver the sons and daughters of the Romans into their hands, so that the Jews may sell them, not to the Persians and Ethiopians and the other nations that are near, but to the Sabeans, a most distant nation, because the Lord has spoken and avenges the injury of his people. So say they and our Judaizers, who promise themselves a thousand-year kingdom within the borders of Judea, and a golden Jerusalem, and the blood of victims, and sons and grandsons and incredible delights, and gates adorned with a variety of gems. But let us say that the Lord both raised up after his coming, and raises up daily, and will raise up those whom manifold error had led out of their borders. […]

3:8.t: Behold, I will raise them up from the place in which you sold them, and I will turn your recompense upon your head, and I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah; and they will sell them to the Sabeans, a nation far off, for the Lord has spoken. LXX: Behold, I will raise them up from the place in which you sold them, and I will return your recompense upon your heads, and I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah; and they will sell them into captivity to a nation that is far away, because the Lord has spoken. The Hebrew word Sabaim, which Aquila and Symmachus translated just as it is written, the LXX rendered as captivity, which would more properly mean captives. Now Sabaim is said to be a nation beyond India, to which also belonged the queen of Sheba, who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, of whom Isaiah too speaks: And Sabaim, men of stature, shall pass over to you. […]

3:9.t: Proclaim this among the nations, sanctify war, rouse the strong. Let them approach, let all the men of war go up. Beat your ploughshares into swords, and your mattocks into spears. Let the weak say, I am strong. Burst out and come, all you nations round about, and gather yourselves together; there the Lord will cause your strong ones to fall. LXX: Proclaim these things among the nations, sanctify war, rouse the fighters, bring them up and go up, all you men of war. Beat your ploughshares into swords, and your sickles into spears. Let the strong say, I prevail. Gather yourselves together and come in, all nations round about; and gather yourselves there; let the gentle one be a warrior. This passage is understood in two ways. […]

3:10.t: Would you understand too the strength and courage of this centurion, by which he bears these arms of which we spoke before as not carnal but mighty to God? Hear of the selection by which the King himself marks and approves brave men when he summons them to the spiritual combat. "Let," says He, "the weak say that I am strong;" and: "Let him who is the sufferer become a warrior." You see then that none but sufferers and weak people can fight the Lord's battles, weak indeed with that weakness, rounded on which that centurion of ours in the gospel said with confidence: "For when I am weak, then am I strong," and again, "for strength is made perfect in weakness." Of which weakness one of the prophets says: "And he that is weak among them shall be as the house of David. For the patient sufferer shall fight these wars, with that patience of which it is said "patience is necessary for you that doing the will of God you may receive the reward."
3:10.s: First Conference of Abbot Serenus, Chapter 5

3:12.t: Let them arise and go up into the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the nations round about; put in the sickles, for the harvest is ripe. Come and go down, for the winepress is full; the vats overflow, for their wickedness is multiplied.
